captions.instagram:
How does an aeroplane fly?

An aeroplane is not sucked up into the sky. Its wings turn the air down, and the air pushes the wing up. Tilt a wing until it stalls, pull an airliner of about 78 tonnes apart, and see why a take-off in Leh needs a longer runway.

→ An aeroplane is a tube with two wings, a tail, two engines and wheels.
→ A wing tilts into the air and turns the air downwards. The air pushes the wing up.
→ Tilt too far and the air leaves the top of the wing. Lift falls. That is a stall.
→ In level flight, thrust pushes forward exactly as hard as drag pushes back.
→ Thin hot air gives less lift and thrust, so the take-off run gets longer.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/aeroplaneclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does an aeroplane fly? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
An aeroplane is not sucked up into the sky. Its wings turn the air down, and the air pushes the wing up. Tilt a wing until it stalls, pull an airliner of about 78 tonnes apart, and see why a take-off in Leh needs a longer runway.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/aeroplaneclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/aeroplaneclear

In this video:
• The one-line idea. A wing makes lift by turning the air down.
• The part people get wrong. The air over the top of a wing does not have to rush to meet the air below.
• Lift against drag. In level flight the engines push as hard as the drag pushes back.
• Controls and flaps. The elevator tilts the nose, the ailerons roll, and the rudder yaws.
• The jet and the glide. A turbofan moves a large mass of air a little, which is efficient.
• How we learned. From Cayley's ideas and Lilienthal's gliders to the Wright brothers in 1903, Tata's first Indian licence in 1929 and the Indian Air Force in 1932.
